posts.title: Tea before practice
posts.excerpt: At 05:50 Ines boils the kettle and carries twelve cups to the deck before the bell.
posts.content:
The kettle goes on at ten to six. By then Ines has been up for twenty minutes: she has swept the deck, wiped the dew from the rail and counted twelve cups onto the long tray, one for every guest and none for herself. The bell is not until a quarter to six, but the tea is the part of the morning she will not hand to anyone else.

It began in the first season, 2014, when the lodge had one kettle that took eleven minutes to boil and a teacher who could not sleep. Ines carried the cups out because it was something to do with her hands. Guests came to the deck in their blankets and, without being asked, did not talk. Nobody has ever written that into the timetable, but the first cup is now the way the quiet begins.

The tea is plain: a loose green leaf from a grower in the next valley, water that has stopped boiling for a minute, nothing sweet. She pours it from the kettle into the row of cups along the deck rail and watches the steam go up into the fog below the larches. If it rains the cups move into the hall, to the low table by the wood stove.

There is a small ritual after it. Each guest takes their cup, finds a place on the boards and holds it with both hands until it is cool enough to drink. Nobody checks a phone; the phones are in the basket by the door. At 06:15 Ines walks to the front of the mats and the practice begins, and the empty cups are collected by whoever finishes first.

We are sometimes asked what we teach in the morning practice. The honest answer is that the tea is half of it. A body that has been given something warm to hold, in a cold place, with nothing to decide, tends to settle on its own. The yoga that follows is ninety slow minutes; the cup is the first five.

If you come for a First Light retreat, the cups will be waiting. Bring a wool layer, because the deck is cold before the sun reaches it, and arrive at the rail before the bell.

posts.title: Walking the Larch Ridge
posts.excerpt: Each morning after breakfast, our forest guide Kofi Mensah leads guests along the nine-kilometer ridge loop where mountain fog lifts at eleven to reveal the quiet expanse of Fernhollow Valley.
posts.content:
At ten in the morning, the lodge quietens as breakfast dishes are cleared from the long table. Guests pull on wool sweaters and lace their walking shoes at the entrance of Larch Hill Lane 9. Kofi Mensah stands waiting on the gravel clearing with his wooden staff, watching the grey mist drift slowly through the lower tree canopy. There are twelve of us in total, stepping out at an easy, unhurried pace past the seasoned cedar woodpile that Tomas Eklund keeps stacked neatly against the lodge wall.

The trail begins immediately behind the practice hall, climbing gradually through thick moss and tall, straight larch trunks. This is the nine-kilometer ridge loop, the primary walking route we follow from the lodge alongside the alternative five-kilometer stream path. During the early morning hours, cool air pools heavily in Fernhollow Valley, trapping low clouds beneath the timberline. As our group ascends in single file, the sound of gravel gives way to the muffled tread of damp earth and the distant murmur of stream water falling over stones.

Walking through the forest requires no forced conversation, although guests often speak in quiet murmurs as the path widens. Kofi walks at the front, maintaining an even, rhythmic cadence that allows everyone to breathe deeply without physical strain. Every few hundred meters, he pauses briefly to indicate deer tracks pressed into the mud, clusters of pale mountain lichen, or fragrant droplets of resin on weathered bark. The ascent is steady but forgiving, designed to invigorate the body after morning practice rather than cause fatigue.

Near the five-kilometer point, the path crests onto an open shoulder of the ridge where a weathered wooden bench sits facing out across the expanse of the valley. It is just before eleven o'clock when the group arrives at the clearing. We pause here to rest our legs, drink cold water from our bottles, and watch the morning weather shift across the canopy. Right on time, as the sun warms the upper atmosphere, the thick mountain fog begins to lift. Broad shafts of pale morning light cut through the grey ceiling, burning off the damp vapor and unveiling the green slopes stretching toward the distant valley floor.

Sitting together on the timber bench and surrounding stones, twelve guests share a moment of complete stillness. From this vantage point, no roads or power lines are visible, only endless undulating rows of larches and pines moving gently in the mountain breeze. Without phones or urgent schedules to distract the mind, the simple act of looking across the valley becomes entirely absorbing. By eleven thirty, the mist has dissolved completely into a pale grey-blue sky, and Kofi turns to lead the group along the descending return path.

The second half of the loop winds downward along a gentle gradient established decades ago when the lodge was a working hostel for forestry crews. The walking is effortless now, gravity carrying us steadily back toward home. By twelve twenty, the dark timber siding and covered deck of Yuzuriha Retreat emerge through the trees. Inside, Mateo Ruiz has finished preparing lunch for twelve thirty, ladling hot soup into bowls and placing fresh loaves on the long table. We leave our muddy boots on the rack by the door, wash our hands, and gather together to eat.

posts.title: Supper at half past six
posts.excerpt: Mateo’s one-pot suppers and the bread that rises during the afternoon rest.
posts.content:
Supper is at half past six, and Mateo starts it at noon. The bread is the first job: he mixes the dough before lunch, leaves it to rise through the afternoon rest, and bakes it at five so that the loaf is still warm when it reaches the long table. Guests who nap on the deck sometimes wake to the smell and take it for a dream.

Everything else is one pot. A soup of beans and winter greens, or a stew of roasted roots with barley, or a dal that has been cooking since the walk began. Mateo cooks vegetarian food, with fish on two evenings a week, and the plates are never decorated. He says the point of supper is not to impress anyone but to end the day with something plain and warm.

The long table seats twelve, which is why the lodge has twelve guests. Bowls are passed from hand to hand, and the person nearest the kitchen door ladles. Nobody is asked to sit in a particular place; by the second evening people have chosen anyway and, by the fourth, are sitting beside different neighbours on purpose.

Conversation at supper is allowed, and during the Seven-Day Quiet Retreat it waits until after lunch. After the meal there is tea, and whoever has finished first helps to clear. The kitchen has one sink and one dishcloth, and there is a rota on the door written in Mateo’s small hand.

When you reserve, tell Nadia what you cannot eat. Vegan, gluten-free and nut-free suppers are cooked every week; there is one kitchen, so we cannot promise a kitchen free of every trace. The rest is plain: a bowl, a slice of bread, and the quiet hour that follows.
